issues.legal_issue: A notice to one joint tenant is sufficient to terminate a joint tenancy, and a suit against the surviving joint tenant is not defective for failing to join the deceased joint tenant’s legal representatives.
material_facts: The lease rights were assigned to two assignees expressly as joint tenants, and the lessor accepted the assignment.
One joint tenant died before the ejectment suit was filed.
The lessor gave notice to the surviving joint tenant, and the suit proceeded against that tenant.
issues.conclusion: The notice to one joint tenant was sufficient, and the suit was not bad for non-joinder of the deceased tenant’s legal representatives.
issues.legal_principle: Where a tenancy is joint, notice to one joint tenant is sufficient; on that basis, the suit against the surviving joint tenant was properly framed. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

rule.if: ejectment_suit and joint_tenancy and notice_served_on_one_joint_tenant and other_joint_tenant_deceased

predicates.ejectment_suit: The lessor brought a suit to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.joint_tenancy: The tenancy rights were held jointly by the tenants.
predicates.notice_served_on_one_joint_tenant: The lessor gave termination notice to one of the joint tenants.
predicates.other_joint_tenant_deceased: The other joint tenant had died before the suit was filed.

issues.definition: When an ejectment suit concerns a joint tenancy, notice to one tenant is sufficient and the suit is not defective for non-joinder when the other tenant has died.

issues.legal_issue: The rent-control law does not govern a local authority’s suit to recover its land, and the suit need not be brought in the court designated for rent-control matters.
material_facts: A local authority sought ejectment and vacant possession of land belonging to it.
The suit’s claim was for possession of the land.
The tenant relied on the rent-control law and argued that the suit belonged in the court designated for rent-control matters.
The relevant statutory amendment addressed specified buildings, while the suit concerned the land.
issues.conclusion: The rent-control law did not prevent the local authority from recovering the land, and the suit was properly brought in the City Civil Court rather than the Small Causes Court.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(1), 4(4)(a), and 5(8) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates (Control) Act, 1947, read together, exclude a local authority’s action concerning its land from the Act; section 4(4)(a) addresses specified buildings and does not extend that exclusion to land. The Court relied on Bhatia Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. D. C. Patel, which explained the effect of section 4(1), and Ram Bhagwandas v. Bombay Corporation, which discussed the amendment’s scope. Accordingly, the rent-control court’s jurisdictional requirement did not apply.

predicates.local_authority_ejectment_suit: A local authority brought a suit to eject a person and recover possession.
predicates.land_owned_by_local_authority: The land sought to be recovered belonged to the local authority.
predicates.claim_concerns_land: The claim for possession concerned the land rather than a claim to evict occupants from a building.

issues.definition: When a local authority seeks possession of its land in an ejectment suit, the rent-control law does not apply and the general civil court has jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: An assignee of a lease that included land and buildings cannot claim that the lessor owned only the land and not the buildings.
material_facts: The lessor granted a tenancy of both the land and the buildings standing on it.
The tenants later assigned their lease rights to the appellant, and the lessor accepted the assignment.
The appellant claimed that the lessor’s ownership extended only to the land, not the buildings.
issues.conclusion: The appellant, as assignee, could not deny that the buildings were included in the lessor’s ownership under the lease.
issues.legal_principle: The terms and admissions in the original lease bound the assignee claiming through the original lessees. Because the lease covered both land and buildings, the assignee could not separate the lessor’s ownership of the land from ownership of the buildings. The Court referred to Bhatia Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. D. C. Patel in discussing the lessor’s ownership of leased premises, but distinguished the present lease circumstances.

predicates.assignee_claims_under_lease: A person claimed lease rights through an assignment from the original lessees.
predicates.original_lease_included_land_and_buildin: The original lease granted rights in both the land and the buildings standing on it.

issues.definition: An assignee claiming under a lease that covered land and buildings cannot deny the lessor’s ownership of the buildings.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s inability to remove buildings or deliver vacant possession because the tenant cannot evict subtenants does not defeat the lessor’s right to recover the land.
material_facts: The lease required the tenants to yield up the premises and provided for the lessor to take the land with the buildings if they were not removed.
The appellant had subtenants and argued that the rent-control law prevented their eviction, making delivery of vacant possession impossible.
The lessor sought possession of the site, and the Court did not decide whether the lessor could evict the subtenants.
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s inability to evict subtenants or remove the buildings did not entitle the appellant to defeat the lessor’s claim to possession of the land.
issues.legal_principle: The lease terms allowed the lessor to take possession of the land with the buildings if the tenant did not remove them. The tenant’s asserted inability to evict subtenants did not defeat the lessor’s rights. The Court left open whether the lessor could evict those subtenants and relied on the reasoning in Ram Bhagwandas v. Bombay Corporation concerning a similar inability to deliver vacant possession.

predicates.land_ejectment_suit: The lessor brought a suit to recover possession of the land.
predicates.lease_requires_yielding_up: The lease required the tenant to yield up the premises and allowed the lessor to take the land with buildings remaining on it.
predicates.tenant_cannot_remove_buildings_due_to_su: The tenant could not remove the buildings because the tenant could not evict subtenants occupying them.

issues.definition: When a lease requires the tenant to yield up the premises and subtenants prevent removal of buildings, that inability does not defeat the lessor’s claim to the land.
